title: Can You Make Money Playing Chess? Chess.com & Other Options
subtitle: Where chess prize money really goes, which routes are open to club players, and what to check before you play a game for a stake.
excerpt: Ordinary Chess.com games pay nothing, and its weekly cash events are for titled players. Here are the routes that do pay club players, and the legal questions to check first.
metaDescription: Can you make money playing chess online? Why Chess.com cash prizes mostly go to titled players, and how equal-stake skill matches work instead.

Club players can win prizes in the rating sections of large open tournaments, such as the World Open's under-1200 section.

content.text: Yes, you can make money playing chess, but for most players the money is small and uneven. Chess pays through four routes: prize tournaments, teaching, content, and matches where both players put up a stake. Which one fits depends on your rating, your time and where you live.
Can you make money on Chess.com?

Not from ordinary games. A rated game on Chess.com moves your rating up or down, and no money changes hands. Cash on Chess.com comes from organised prize events, and the regular weekly ones are for titled players.

Titled Tuesday, the best-known weekly event, is open to members whom Chess.com recognises as holding a FIDE title or a national master title, according to its 2026 event rulebook. Up to $10,000 is available in each event, with $2,500 for first place. The same rulebook limits 3 0 Thursday, Freestyle Friday and Bullet Brawl to FIDE or national master titleholders.

A few events, such as Arena Kings, are open to all members in good standing, each with its own prize conditions. For an untitled player, Chess.com is mainly a place to improve and build a playing record, not a source of income.
Four ways chess players earn money
1. Rating sections at open tournaments

Large open tournaments split players into rating sections, so a club player competes against people of similar strength. The 2026 World Open, run by the Continental Chess Association, offered $4,000 for first place in its under-1200 section, and its under-1200 and under-1000 sections together guaranteed $17,000 in prizes. Entry fees, travel and several days of games come first, and most entrants finish outside the prize places.
2. Coaching and lessons

For most strong amateurs, teaching pays more reliably than playing. Beginners need someone who explains ideas clearly more than they need a grandmaster, so a patient club player can coach newer players. Rates and demand vary widely by country and by platform.
3. Streaming, videos and writing
Content earns from ads, subscriptions and sponsors, and it rewards personality and consistency as much as rating. It takes time to build an audience before it pays.
4. Equal-stake matches

On some platforms, two players each put up the same amount before the game, and the winner takes most of the pot. This is the only route where a single game decides the money, so it suits players who already win more than they lose at a given time control. It also means you can lose your stake in any game.
Is playing chess for money gambling?
There is no single worldwide answer. Chess has no dice or shuffled cards, and every move is a player's choice, but the law where you live decides how a paid match is treated.

In the United States, much of gambling law is set by each state. Most states use some form of the dominant factor test, which asks whether skill or chance mainly decides the result. Not every state agrees. Colorado's Supreme Court took a broader view of chance in 1989, and in 2012 South Carolina's Supreme Court held that what counts is whether something of value is wagered, not the balance of skill and chance. Other countries have their own definitions.

Before you play for money anywhere, read the platform's terms and check your local rules. Web3Chess requires players to be at least 18, or older where local law sets a higher age, and availability depends on local rules and in-app eligibility.
This article is general information, not legal advice. If you are unsure how the law applies where you live, ask a qualified local adviser before you play for a stake.
How a stake match works in Web3Chess

Web3Chess runs chess inside Telegram and in the browser. Every game against another person carries a stake, while games against Free Coach, the computer opponent, are free. The full details are on the [USDT match rules](/wagers) page.

items: Both players commit the same USDT stake from their app balance before the first move. Lobby presets run from 1 to 1,000 USDT, a custom amount is allowed, and the minimum is 1 USDT.

In a decided game, the winner's app balance is credited with 95% of the combined pot. On a 10 USDT stake, that is 19 USDT, a net gain of 9 USDT. The other 5% is a 3% platform fee and a 2% referral allocation.
A draw by stalemate, threefold repetition, the 50-move rule or agreement returns both stakes in full, with no fee.
If a clock runs out while the opponent cannot checkmate, the game is a draw and both stakes are refunded.
If a player does not make a first move within 30 seconds, the match is aborted and both stakes are refunded.
Withdrawals are requested in the app and confirmed in the Telegram bot chat. Larger requests also wait for a manual review.

content.text: Should you play for money? A quick check

items: Practise first. Play Free Coach at the clock you plan to use, and check whether you convert winning positions without losing on time.
Pick one time control and stay with it. A shorter clock leaves less time to check each move, so results can swing more from game to game.
Set a limit before you start. Decide the most you are willing to lose in a session, stop when you reach it, and never chase losses.
Only stake money you can afford to lose. Winning a handful of games proves little about your long-run results.
